utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Jadranko Prlic et al., thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. Today is Thursday, October 30, 2008. I wish good morning to everybody, to the accused. I see that Mr. Pusic is not here. I wish him a prompt recovery. I wish a good morning to the Defence counsel, to Mr. Scott, and Mr. Kruger, his deputy, and also everybody else assisting us in this case. First of all, I would like to issue an oral decision, a formal oral decision since we've already discussed the matter, but we needed to be more specific in issuing an oral decision, so I will read slowly. Oral decision regarding the Prosecution request to delete Mr. Neven Tomic from the Defence witness list or alternatively to postpone his appearance before the Court until such time a more comprehensive 65 ter summary and its discussion with Mr. Cvikl are disclosed. On October the 15th, the Prosecution filed a motion to forbid or postpone the appearance of witness Neven Tomic until such time a more comprehensive 65 ter summary is provided and its discussions with Milan Cvikl are disclosed. The testimony of witness Neven Tomic began on October the 27th, 2008. During the hearing held on October the 20th, 2008, the Prlic Defence informed the Trial Chamber that it did not have the statements relating to discussions between Neven Tomic and Milan Cvikl. First of all, the Chamber recalls that it had already declared moot the application made by the Prosecution to receive a more comprehensive 65 ter summary in its oral decision issued on October 20th, 2008. Secondly, and having heard the response of the Prlic Defence, the Chamber has decided to dismiss the Prosecution's application regarding the communication of discussions between Mr. Neven Tomic and Mr. Milan Cvikl. Since there was no notes, they can't be disclosed. I would like now to have the witness brought into the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness isn't here there is a matter that can be conveniently dealt with. Your Honours may recall that the Defences -- or four of the Defences jointly filed a motion I think it was on the 10th of this month relating to use of exhibits by the Prosecution and introduction of new exhibits during cross-examination. There has been a response from the Prosecution. Your Honour, the response as the initial motion is just under 4.000 words. It's a fairly meaty document. Your Honour, it does call for a reply. We do need leave for a reply, and we ask you if Your Honours would give us that leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Given the interest of this issue, of course you are granted leave to reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Tomic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The cross-examination will now continue. I give the floor to Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good morning to you. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. Mr. Tomic, good morning. I think I have about 20 minutes left in light of the fact that the Defence has slightly more than four hours all told, but before we continue with the cross-examination I would just like to respond to the objection raised by my colleague Mr. Scott that 63 leading questions were asked and that the witness said yes 63 times in response to those leading questions. The questioning of Mr. Tomic and his responses have shown that the discussion about economy and money would lead us to the very essence of the case and will help us determine the centres of power that existed in the HZ HB, and his examination has shown that those centres of power were located primarily in the municipalities whose presidents were at the same time members of the legislative body of the HZ HB. It is quite clear to me that the responses given by this witness are not something that the Prosecutor is happy to hear, and that is why I see Mr. Scott's response as an attempt to diminish the importance and the value of Mr. Tomic's testimony. That is why I do not take seriously the objection raised by Mr. Scott that each yes or no answer is a worthless answer to a leading question, because if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought you'd finished. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to provide some more explanations. I think this is a major issue because Mr. Scott has repeatedly raised such objections. If we ask the witness if in 1993 Croats and Muslims signed a peace agreement and then the witness says yes, I think that this is not a worthless question to a leading -- worthless answer to a leading question. If a Judge tries to sum up the witness's testimony and then asks the witness if this is a correct interpretation of his testimony and then if a witness answers yes, this is correct, I don't think again this is a worthless answer to a leading question regardless of who actually asks the question. The witness has replied affirmatively to a number of facts which could be deemed as notorious in this case, and that is that the representatives of the Bosnian Croats and Muslims signed the Washington Agreement, that the Washington Agreement envisaged a joint government based on the principle of parity, that this agreement envisaged a Joint Command over the two armies, the BH army and the HVO, again based on the principle of parity. The fact that is also uncontroversial is that Alija Izetbegovic at one point signed the Vance-Owen Plan, so is the fact that the HVO HZ HB at one point became the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, the functions held by Mr. Boban are not in contention, and I will not now list all of those facts that I firm believe are notorious by this time. Some of the affirmative answers provided by this witness had to do with his previous evidence or statements, and some of the answers had to do with the documents that were shown to this witness. The contents of these documents make it possible to evaluate the accuracy of the answers provided by this witness, and we can conclude that the answers are fully in line with the contents of the documents shown to the witness. In light of all that I have now said, it appears that perhaps it was not quite clear to Mr. Scott and maybe to some others. Well, I will now show the witness a document that we have discussed both during the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Before we move on, we must provide some kind of an answer to what you said. First of all, I'll give the floor to Mr. Scott and then the Trial Chamber will add something.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning to each of Your Honours, and good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom, counsel. With great respect to my friend Ms. Alaburic, the comments -- her comments on the merits of the case and the merits of the substance of the answers has absolutely nothing to do with the procedural point that the Prosecution feels is very important. Ms. Alaburic very capably gets on her feet and starts arguing the merits of her case. I was proving this, this will show the crux of the case, this will show this, this will show that. That's completely, completely irrelevant for this purpose. The issue here is a procedural one. It's a matter of fundamental fairness in the way that the trial is being conducted, with great respect to the Chamber, and it's the Prosecution continuing view and we know the Chamber's ruled but we will continue to make a record on this with the greatest respect to the Judges, that this is a fundamentally unfair procedure to the Prosecution. It is -- I have called it before, I may have said it in this courtroom, I may have not. The manner in which the co-accused are being allowed to put questions to witnesses is I would consider it the perfect unfairness machine. It is the perfect unfairness machine. It's hard to imagine a less fair process. Additional time is given to the Defence which doesn't count against their time. The Prosecution gets no additional time. With this witness the Prosecution gets 12 hours, four of which are not count against anyone's time. The Prosecution gets eight hours. The Defence is allowed to proceed by leading questions to a friendly witness, again no additional opportunity for the Prosecution to be able to respond, no additional time for the Prosecution to be able to respond to that, no indication from the co-accused as to what the nature of that examination testimony will be. Therefore, we're close with this witness and I predict there may come with a time with future witnesses, for example, where the Prosecution will have to ask to suspend or delay cross-examination, its cross-examination so it can have adequate time to respond to issues raised for the first time with no notice, because there is no notice, from the co-accused. There are a variety of issues, Your Honour, that are raised by this procedure, and it is indeed -- it is, I would say, very close to the perfect unfairness machine to the Prosecution. No time, no -- leading questions to a friendly witness, just a whole host of matters. It would be hard to design a less -- a less fair system to the Prosecution. Now, again the -- Ms. Alaburic' comments on the merits have nothing to do with the arguments here, and it has nothing to do with Prosecution's happiness or not happiness with the answers. That is really insulting, frankly, when any counsel makes that point. I don't -- I'm sure no one in the courtroom cares if Ken Scott with the Prosecution is happy with the answers or not just as I don't care whether the Defence is happy with the answers or not. That's completely beside the point. We're talking here about procedural, fundamental procedural matters and fairness to the parties and fairness to the Prosecution and its ability to receive a fair trial. There is a very substantial difference, there is a very substantial difference and Judge Trechsel at least has observed this himself on some occasions that is very substantial difference in an open, narrative answer by a witness in which many things come across, nuance, limitation, qualification, detail. Perhaps the witness is uncertain. Well, I can say this much but I can't say that. All sorts of things that come out in a narrative answer that you do not -- neither the Chamber nor the Prosecution gets when the answer is simply yes, yes, yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Don't do it 63 times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I won't do it 63 times, I'll stop there. It's a fundamentally different process and all you have to do is compare the answers given by anyone. It's not just Mr. Tomic but any answer which he says well, I can't say that or I'm not sure or maybe I can say this much but more or no. It's a completely different process, Your Honour, and that is what we're working with here and that is why this process, with the greatest respect to the Chamber, is unfair and frankly not only unfair to the Prosecution but deprives the Chamber, deprives the Judges of valuable evidence that it doesn't get by simply yes, yes, yes, yes, yes. So, Your Honour, that's -- that's our position. I would also note just in passing, although it's not our fundamental position at this time, that the question put now, the pending question, as it were, about the Vance-Owen Plan, excuse me, was not a topic raised by Mr. Karnavas as far as I recall. We talked about the Washington Agreement some. I think we talked about Dayton a little bit, but I don't remember talking at all about the Vance-Owen Plan which is again an example of the point of questioning by the co-accused on topics that were not raised for which the Prosecution has no notice. I didn't -- let me just be very clear. Over the past week I have not -- I have been trying to guess -- the Prosecution is put in the position of trying to guess what the cross -- what the testimony might be with no information as to the question of what the co-accused will be. Now the Vance-Owen Peace Plan has been raised. I am not prepared, and I'm not asking anyone to shed tears, I am not prepared to conduct cross-examination on Vance-Owen Plan. I haven't put Vance-Owen Plan documents in our bundles. I can't do that on 10 minutes' notice. I can't give the Chamber 15 copies of hard copy documents on the spur of the moment on topics that are just raised. It raises a variety of points, Your Honour, and I think on that particular question, and that's when I rose to my feet, it was inappropriate. Counsel is clear, there maybe some things that are not disputed, some basic facts of the case, so to speak. If they're not disputed, you know, counsel can't have it both ways. They're either disputed or they're not disputed, but if they're not disputed they don't need to be put to the witness simply by leading questions. No one -- no one in the courtroom questions that Mate Boban was the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, no one. It's absolutely undisputed. So it's -- there's no point in putting -- there's no point in saying well, I'm only going over matters that are not disputed. If they're not disputed there's no reason to put them to the witness. So Your Honour with that all that, that states our concerns and the position of the Prosecution on these matters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may just have one moment. We've taken up 20 minutes of time now in front of the witness on this issue. There is a continuing objection from the Prosecution to these matters. I don't think that it's necessary to stand up all the time. I would suggest, I would suggest, because there are some valid points that are being made on all sides, I don't necessarily agree with everything that everybody is saying, but this is a sort of procedural issue that should be dealt with perhaps through a special hearing, either 65 ter outside the courtroom, but I just think that to have these sort of objections and procedural issues raised over and over again while the witness is here away from his family and home, and we're trying to get the evidence on and the witness back, I just think we're wasting a lot of valuable time in the courtroom. Though I do take everybody's point at hand, but we may just want to deal with this at a separate hearing.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, please allow me. I think I do have the right to respond to the second round of the objections raised by Mr. Scott. The time that I will take up to do that can be deducted from my time allotted for the cross-examination, because I fully agree with what Mr. Karnavas said about not keeping the witness longer than necessary here in The Hague. As far as leading questions in cross-examination are concerned, I think that Mr. Scott is unjustified in raising this issue yet again after the Trial Chamber has already ruled on this issue and allowed leading questions in the cross-examination by the Defence. I think that our learned friends from the Prosecution, by re-raising this objection, insult the Trial Chamber. If the Prosecution believes that the decision by the Trial Chamber is not fair or lawful, the Prosecution can ask the Trial Chamber to take into account, to consider the issue once again and then take further measures. Until this is done, I move that the Trial Chamber prohibit the Prosecution from raising the standing objection again and again during the cross-examination of the Defence. And I would like to also note here that the Prosecution has here mixed up the issue of friendly witnesses and leading questions in cross-examination. We have already dealt with this in a motion that we filed. Secondly, as regards the time allotted to the cross-examination to the Prosecution and the Defence, I object once again, and I protest against the fact that the Defence is treated as a whole. I don't want the Petkovic Defence to be treated as such. I would like to -- us to be treated as a single entity, separate entity. In accordance with the Rules of Procedure and Evidence each of the accused is accorded the same right in this case as if they were tried separately. The Petkovic Defence is not happy with the time allotted for its cross-examination because we only have six -- one-sixth of the time that the Prosecution has. Secondly, as regards this objection raised by the Prosecution in which they claim they are not accorded a fair trial, I would like to remind the Judges that no international covenant on human rights or any other international treaty does not guarantee the Prosecution the right to a fair trial. The right to a fair trial is the one that is given to an accused, and that is why there are different procedural mechanisms in place to protect the rights of the accused to the presumption of innocence and other rights. As regards the concern expressed by my learned friend Mr. Scott that the Judges might be misled regarding some questions and answers, well, I don't doubt that the Judges will be able to give proper weight to each and every answer including those given to leading questions. I'm fully cognisant of the fact that answers provided to leading questions are less well valuable than those given to open-ended questions, but I also know this: If an answer given to a leading question is corroborated by a number of documents and answers given by other witnesses, then the answer given to these leading questions -- question has great weight. As regards the part of my cross-examination that deals with the Vance-Owen Plan, I have to say that I did not ask a single question. I do not intend to ask any questions about the Vance-Owen Plan. I will ask this witness about the plan for the visit to the municipalities in April 1993. Once I'm done with this document it will be quite clear that I'm not raising the topic of the contents of the Vance-Owen Plan, but I will follow up on the part of the cross-examination where we determine that the witness visited parts and municipalities of Herceg-Bosna and was aware of the situation in the field. This is all I have to say in my response. I would like to thank you, Your Honours, for the time you've given me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On those numerous issues that were raised and which go in various directions, the Chamber has already issued decisions, provided guidelines. The Chamber ruled that the accused, the co-accused, can during the cross-examination ask questions to the witness of another accused. Now, this raises the issue whether leading questions should be asked or, rather, neutral ones. On that issue, since it is a cross-examination within the Anglo-Saxon exception of the term, questions may be of a leading nature, but if it is a cross-examination, i.e., the follow-up questions on first cross-examination, then of course questions should not be leading. And, Mrs. Alaburic, you are right. You are right. We give more weight to the answer to a question that's not leading and less weight when the question was leading. This is a technical matter, if I may say so. Mr. Scott observed that 63 times the witness said yes. In order to avoid this maybe you should use another method, i.e., when you've listened to the witness's answer, you could try and sum up the question, sum up the answer, and then ask an open question so that the witness has the opportunity to say yes, no, or to provide other information. Take an example: Document 1D 02003. You could have said this is a document that wasn't used by Mr. Karnavas although he initially planned to do so, it is a programme of the visits in the various municipalities, can you have a look at the document. Then the witness will say yes. Then you could ask could you please tell the Trial Chamber what this document is about and then the witness will say well, this document is a programme for ten visits organised by various people including me and so on and so forth. Then you could ask the witness why were such visits organised and then the witness will answer, well, this document talks about municipalities 3, 8, and 10, and then we-- we distributed those municipalities among themselves, and then you will say what about these municipalities, what are there, and then you will be talking about the Vance-Owen Plan, and then you ask what is this plan, according to you, and then maybe you can conclude this line of questioning with a question that may be leading: Isn't that proof that this document shows that as of the 9th of May you implemented the various aspects of the Vance-Owen Plan and then he will say yes or he will say no and then maybe he will supplement his answer. It is a technical issue. My colleague Judge Trechsel would like the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to go back to the issue of leading questions, but first I look at what in the transcript on page 11, lines 20 and following to 25 is written down, and I've heard that you have actually said that. I wonder, Ms. Alaburic, whether you are really serious in saying that, that there is no fair trial for the Prosecution but only for the Defence. You are right if you refer to the covenants, but we have a Statute, and I would have supposed that you know the Statute, which in Article 20 clearly charges the Court, the Chamber, with seeing to it that the trial is fair. And we have a number of case law, very clear-cut case law of the Chamber of Appeals of this Tribunal which clearly says that a trial cannot be fair if fairness is granted only to the Defence. So I am really surprised that you could tell the Chamber something like this. And if you're talking about disrespect to the Chamber, I think this is closer than what you accused the accusation, the Prosecutor of doing. I'm a bit shocked, I must say, by such words. Now, as to leading questions, we have already decided that leading questions should not be posed in the so-called cross-examination when in fact it is nothing but the continuation of direct, and at one point you have said, and I think it was in relation to document 1D 02003, there is one document Mr. Karnavas didn't have enough time to cover so I'll take it up. Now, where is fairness if you pretend that in direct Mr. Karnavas would have had to ask open question, whereas now you taking over the same document and the same issue are allowed to ask leading questions? That defies any logic and any concept of fairness. And indeed basically the accusation is right in saying that you should when you go in the same direction as the main counsel to his witness, then you should not change the modes and ask leading questions all through because that would really be unfair.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for these clarifications and the positions you have put forward. If you allow, I will reply to the considerations and the position of His Honour Judge Trechsel. First about document 1D 02003. If you look at all documents which the Defence of Mr. Prlic has handed in for the interrogation of this witness, you will not find that document among them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Alaburic. Could you stay with the facts? I have not said that it had been put. I have quoted you. You said Mr. Karnavas didn't have the time to go into this document. You can look it up.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I literally said, and I carefully pick every word I utter in this courtroom, I said that this document was initially prepared for the interrogation of this witness, but it was left out from the last chart, and as I think that this document contains some important facts, I shall deal with it. These were my words literally, unless they were rendered differently in English. If that is the case, I will listen to the tape once more and ask for a correction of the transcript. As for the interrogation of the witness about that document, I must first say that my questioning about this document had only started, then we started speaking about various things. I have not completed questioning the witness about this document. I was interested in whether the witness remembers that the programme was adopted, whether he remembered the government session where it was adopted, whether he really visited the municipalities, and the document reads that the intention was to familiarise the people on the ground with the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. Therefore, I think that this is not a leading question but simply a joint reading of the document. Secondly, about the right to a fair trial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Alaburic, with all respect I think now you are discussing the decision of the Chamber and you should -- yes, of the Bench, and you should not do that. I'm thinking back of what Mr. Karnavas reasonably said, and I think you should continue with the examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Honourable Judge, I care much about your opinion, and I appreciate your position, and if you say that you're shocked by anything I said, I have the purely human need to explain, and this is about the fairness of the trial and the right to a fair trial. That's a topic we could discuss for hours, a topic with which I have dealt extensively in my country. In my opinion there is a difference between the right to a fair trial as a guaranteed human right and the right of a citizen and the notion of a fair trial in the sense of devising a concrete procedure and setting rules for it. When we say the right to a fair trial, I always understand that to mean a human and civil right, and such a right in no country is guaranteed to the Prosecution but only to the indicted. If we discuss another concept, namely fair trial, then an elementary rule is that procedural rules must be defined so that both or several parties to a proceeding have the same right to be able to prove their arguments. I believe that our understanding of these terms does not differ. I do not question the -- that -- I don't put it to question that this procedure should be fair toward all parties to the proceeding, including the Prosecution. We would not be satisfied with the proceedings if the Prosecution did not have the right to put forward all its arguments in enough time and elaborate them the way it thinks fit. I would like to remind that the Defence of General Petkovic has always supported the Prosecution when it asked for additional time to question one of its witnesses or asked for -- for additional time for new witnesses once it had been denied to them. We have always reacted in such a manner. I believe that we have clarified all possible misunderstanding and that we can continue to question the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mrs. Alaburic. Continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That said, if you address a new topic which has not been addressed by Mr. Karnavas, put questions that are not leading.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will do that, but when I return to this document, I will say why I think that this document bears upon the topics raised in the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, yesterday I thought about your replies to my questions and tried to evaluate them, my questions that were leading, and you mostly answered yes or no, and I thought -- I think I've shown why nothing else was possible, but I think that my question and your reply were left suspended in midair, so to speak, why you, when we speak about the highest of priority you meant the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the part that it concerned the HZ HB. You answered affirmatively. Please look up document 1D 1934 in my set of documents. That is your document on the functioning of the financial system, dated August 12, 1993. Would you please read to us the end of the last sentence in the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "As such conduct is on the rise, at least since the collapse of the newly established system, we are forced into discussion with heads of finance departments of municipal HVOs at a meeting held on 4 August 1993 in Ljubuski and subsequently at a meeting with representatives of municipalities held at Siroki Brijeg on 5 August to warn them of such conduct and consequences it may cause for our community, which may eventually affect the defence of the areas of the Croatian people in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please slow down for the sake of the interpretation. Tell me, Mr. Tomic, why are you mentioning the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in this document or to be more precise the defence of the area of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our activities we never neglected the fact that the areas in which the Croatian people lives is part of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that it is -- it constituents part of the state of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us return to the document where we stopped our cross-examination, and that's document 1D 02003, and that is a programme of the visit to the municipalities which adopted by the HZ HB on April the 9th, 1993. Tell us, Mr. Tomic, in the direct you were answering to questions pertaining to the establishment of a joint government headed by Mr. Jadranko Prlic about the correspondence between Jadranko Prlic with Alija Izetbegovic about the establishment of that government. Tell me how that to do with the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan or with some other territorial organisation.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had to do with the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Is it visible from this document what your duties were?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us which the -- they were?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our duty was to go to these provinces, that is the municipalities and the provinces put forward by the Vance-Owen Plan and to familiarise them with the content of the Vance-Owen Plan and to prepare the heads of the municipalities for the reorganisation of the system in line with the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you at the HVO meeting before going to the ground, did you speak about this organisation of work and the Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The meeting took place on the 3rd of April, and the -- it was about the programme adopted on the 9th of -- which was later adopt on the 9th of April and prepare everybody who had to be involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: After this visit to the municipalities, did the HVO HZ HB plan to -- plan any other activities for the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an initial activity that we had to launch so as to implement the agreement. Subsequent activities depended on whether or not the basic issue was implemented, namely the establishment of the central government at the republican level.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: As you participated in these activities, did you personally sincerely believe and want the Vance-Owen Plan to be implemented?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said so already. We really were very sincere in our intention regarding the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan or any other plan that would put an end to the war, because we knew that in the long term we would be unable to preserve the system which was created as a temporary one. I said that in 1994 we had 130.000 budget beneficiaries, speaking about salaries only, and any other solution of -- for the functioning of the system would have been a more favourable variant. That's why we had a genuine interest in the implementation of such a plan and at this time the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answers. There is another topic that I feel, Mr. Tomic, you are the best witness to address this with. In the examination-in-chief you mentioned that the political option that the Muslims from Bosnia-Herzegovina advocated was a centralised state based on the principle of one man, one vote. Is this what you said verbatim to Mr. Prlic's Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please tell us, what was the option that was advocated by the Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The option that was advocated by the BH Croats was put forward at the time when the referendum, question for the referendum for the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina was being formulated. The BH Croats supported the independence, and they wanted and they expected that Bosnia-Herzegovina would be established as a community in which all three constituent peoples would have equal rights. This has always been our political option.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us clarify this community of three constituent peoples. Did that mean that the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina would have to be set up as a federation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have moved on to another subject. I would like to stick with the document we saw a while ago before talking about constituent people. This is a follow-up. Now, you shared the work out when you went to visit these municipalities. You went to the third [Realtime transcript read in error "Serb"] municipality. I can see here that Mr. Prlic was asked to go to Mostar. I realise that this programme of visits was then cut down and should only last three days. Was this because a briefing had been planned?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you allow me, let me correct the transcript. At line 9 it is stated that you said that Mr. Tomic was charged with going to Serb municipalities. The -- what we received in the Croatian interpretation is the province number 3.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The third municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said debriefing, not briefing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the plan envisages that those activities should end by the 16th of April for a very simple reason, in order to be able to plan further activities of the HVO HZ HB, because its members were supposed to go out in the field and the effort was made to do all this within a certain period of time in order to be able to continue with the activities, the sessions of the HVO HZ HB. It was my task to go to the municipalities in province number 3. Unfortunately, at that time there was only one municipality that was controlled by the Croatian Defence Council, the municipality of Orasje in the Bosnian Posavina, and together with Mr. Stipo Ivankovic who hails from that area I went there and I spoke to the people in the municipality of Orasje. I took that opportunity to check how things were functioning on the ground, especially in terms of the financial system. All the more so because this area was an island where -- an isolated area where the HZ HB regulations were in force. This area, it was the easiest for that area to move on to the application of the Vance-Owen Plan in terms of the provinces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm interested is -- in is this: In Orasje how did the municipality receive this plan? They must have asked questions. Was this an advantage or not? Would all the problems be solved with this plan? What did the future hold? The people you met, were they enthusiastic? Were they skeptical? Did they have reservations? Were they reticent when you exposed this plan to them? What did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The area of the Bosnian Posavina is well-known for the cooperation between Muslims and Croats in the defence effort, and really there were no obstacles for the implementation of this plan based on the response of the people from the municipality of Orasje and the people who had fled there from other municipalities in province number 3 who were now staying in Orasje. That was my perception after my visit there. Let me just illustrate, give you an example. The boats that were used to take us from Croatia into Bosnia-Herzegovina flew the flags of the HZ HB and of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and at that time I would say there was a great deal of positive anticipation. They felt that this would put a stop to any tensions and would make it possible to build the system as it was envisaged in the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You must have held a meeting with Zubak, Valenta, Buntic, Perkovic, Maric, Prlic, and other people during your visit. Was there an overall impression which people shared after this visit? Were people very favourable towards this plan, had a moderate view, were reticent? What was the general feeling about this plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The general impression was positive. For the most part the remarks made had to do with the parity, that we should insist on the parity that was envisaged in the Vance-Owen Plan, but the feeling was that the Croats were ready to implement the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let me follow up on what His Honour Judge Antonetti said to conclude this topic. What was this internal organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina that the representatives of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina wanted? I'm talking about the period in -- period of 1992, 1993.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was a system or an organisation that would take on board the fact that the Croats, despite the fact that they were in the minority in Bosnia and Herzegovina, would get a solution that would guarantee equal rights to them, that they would be equal with the other peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In other words, that they should not be out-voted -- or, rather, that there should not be a state based on the principle of one man, one vote, which would lead to them being out-voted. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correctly. That is why I said that there was this corollary to the referendum question that the Croats used when they expressed their free will at this referendum. Yes, an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina, but which would not result in less rights for Croats and that would have been the result if the one vote, one man principle would be applied.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, you used to be an official in the youth organisation in the old system.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we then conclude that you were quite familiar with the Yugoslav political system?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now I would like you to help me explain to the Judges something that I think is very important. How come that Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the socialist Yugoslavia, was able to function as a unitary state, yet after Yugoslavia broke down this was no longer possible, at least in accordance with the views presented by the Croat representatives? And we know that the representatives of Serbs had the same or similar views. Let me ask you this question I'm sure that you'll be able to answer. In socialist Yugoslavia was there a socio-political organisation that was called the League of Communists of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, this League of Communists of Yugoslavia, was this an integrative factor in the political organisation of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: An integrative factor in the Yugoslav political community. Do you recall the Congress of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, that the Slovenian delegation left and the Croatian delegation left the hall but remained in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember this event.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the comments at the time that this marked the beginning of the end of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia and most likely the beginning of the breakdown of the Yugoslav society, the Yugoslav state?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, at the time when Yugoslavia broke up and when Bosnia and Herzegovina became an independent state, was there a similar integrative factor in Bosnia-Herzegovina or was there no such integrative factor in terms of some political organisation or any other institution? Perhaps let me ask you another question. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, the League of Communists, did it have the kind of personnel policy that made sure that Croats, Muslims and Serbs and representatives of other peoples would have -- would be assigned to various functions on the principle of parity?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the case. I know that in Mostar, the Mostar municipality, the president of the socialist league, the president of the trade union, the president of the municipality, the president of the youth organisation, the president of the war veterans organisation, those were the functions where the League of Communists decided whom to appoint, and this was done on the basis of the ethnicity. And if the mayor or the president of the municipality was a Croat at one point, he was succeeded by a Serb or a Muslim and the functions were rotated in this manner. Out of the eight functions three belonged to Croats, three to Muslims, two to Serbs, and there was this rotation in addition to this so that each people had their representatives in the government.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was this a way to ensure the equality of all the constituent peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this manner this was implemented in that system.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: At the first multi-party election in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the end of 1991 the nationalist parties, the ethnicity-based parties won. A leading question but you can also say no. Does that mean that at that time in Bosnia-Herzegovina the integrative factor that could through the personnel policy or in any other way would guarantee the equality of the constituent peoples disappear, that they disappear at that time?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time the parties that won the election for all intents and purposes started taking care of their peoples within Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you recall the amendments to the constitutions of Bosnia and Herzegovina in late 1991 when the composition of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina was changed? The rule that the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina should comprise -- I'm now talking off the top of my head but I'll let my colleagues correct me if I'm wrong but by the end of 1991 the rule was that three representatives should be from the Muslim ethnic community, two from the Serb community, one from the Croat community and there would be one representative of other ethnic groups, and at one point this solution was replaced by a provision that the Presidency of the BH should comprise two representatives of each constituent people, Muslims, Serbs, and Croats, and one representative of other ethnic groups. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the Presidency was constituted in this manner, but I don't recall those changes. I do remember that there were two Croats, two Muslims or Bosniaks, and two Serbs and one representative of other ethnic groups of Yugoslav.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me whether the representatives of the Croat people wanted Bosnia and Herzegovina to be set up as a complex state comprising several constituent units and that each of those constituent units should be set up in such a way that the criterion of ethnicity be taken into account and that then those constituent units would reach a consensus at the state level and decide on all key national interests and rights on the basis of this consensus which would prevent the representatives of any of the peoples from out-voting the representatives of the other peoples?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in that context.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this has completed my cross-examination. Mr. Tomic, I would like to thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tomic, I have a follow-up question. I was very interested by the question asked on the Communist League of which you were a member and on the issue of disintegration linked to the 1991 elections, and in the questions and answers you provided I felt that the political parties which took part in the 1991 elections were parties based on ethnicity rather than on particular political or economic platforms. According to you, what was the reason for this, for the fact that some parties were more based on ethnicity than on political platforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My personal opinion is that the Communist system over a long period of time tried to build an artificial nation, the Yugoslav nation and eliminating other nations or ethnic groups in the process. In other words, the number of Croats, Serbs, and the Muslims would decree at the expense of the Yugoslavs whose number would rise. This concept, of course, engendered a certain degree of dissatisfaction, but while the Communist Party was strong and while it had mechanisms of coercion at its disposal the function -- the system functioned, but it engendered a great deal of dissatisfaction, discontent among the people, particularly if we add to this mix that -- that religious communities were excluded from public life, and this caused some frustration for them, and I think that at the time when this system in Yugoslavia was at its lowest point, was at its weakest, economically first of all, that the forces that had suffered this frustration got stronger, and they simply destroyed this concept that the Communist Party had been building for such a long time. Let me go back to Mostar to illustrate this point. According to the 1991 census, there was a substantial percentage of Yugoslavs in Mostar. It was a city where there were four or five barracks of the Yugoslav People's Army. In accordance with this concept advocated by the Communist Party it was an integrative factor. It was a key element of this sense of Yugoslavdom. There was Soko defence industry in Mostar. People from all other Yugoslavia worked there. They were assigned to go there. And when the pre-election campaign was under way, at the city stadium we had the same number of followers or people who had come to follow the campaign for all the parties, the SDA, the HDZ, the SDS, but the same also went for the Reformist Party and the SDP party, the party that was the successor of the Communist Party. So this was a phenomenon in Mostar that told me that people didn't know how to -- what to decide and how all this would come out, but the -- when the election results came in you could see that there was a landslide victory for the ethnicity-based parties. So the question was over a course of maybe 15 or 20 days between the rallies that were organised by the SDP and The reformists, where had all the Yugoslavs gone? Because those parties did not get the votes of the Yugoslavs at the municipal election. The people voted for -- as I've already explained to you, the group of frustrated people, and after the elections the picture that emerged gave a clear right to the SDA, the HDZ, and the SDS to set up the city government, and the remaining two parties did not participate in the establishment of the government. Something similar happened at the level of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. See how a non-leading question can lead to a very long answer? Who is next?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Tomic. Mr. Tomic, you can confirm that we've known each other for a number of years and we know each other well, but we haven't spoken about the documents I'm about to show.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That means I'll need a little more time, but as I'm going to dwell upon matters regarding financing almost exclusively, I believe that this will shorten the procedure. Before I start, I would like to follow up on the question asked by Ms. Alaburic about the organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina according to the wishes and the -- and the visions of the three peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina. You said what the wish of the Croatian people was. We know that throughout the conflict there has been this disparity between the interpretation of the Sarajevo government on the other hand and the HZ HB on the other hand about the organisation of the future Bosnia-Herzegovina. If you could, briefly outline to the Chamber whether that problem still exists today. You used to take part in politics, and nowadays you are a citizen, and I know that you're -- you are still interested in politics. You are a political person. The problem of Bosnia, which still cannot start functioning due to the continuing conflict of these concepts in Bosnia, is it still around in spite of all the declarations of agreeing to the present-day organisation of Bosnia? Does the Croatian people still have a problem with realising the position it was -- it has been promised since 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My personal view of the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina today is completely in accordance with the high representatives of the international community especially the High Rep and other people who had been involved in matters in Bosnia-Herzegovina before. The political situation is very bad. The satisfaction of all three peoples due -- the elections held so far has asserted -- have asserted the domination of ethnic parties, which to me shows that there is still dissatisfaction with the organisation of the state and that there are continuing attempts to strive for protection through strengthening ethnic homogeneity instead of opting for people with a programme and a vision that are able to introduce Bosnia-Herzegovina into the community of European peoples and the international community. We keep speaking about constitutional change, and it's a fact that the Croats are marginalised in Bosnia-Herzegovina with regard to their influence. Bosnia-Herzegovina under the Dayton Accord was organised as a compound of two entities. In the federation there have been changes as compared to the Washington Agreement which guaranteed parity and protection, but in the federation that principle has been abandoned due to the demands by the Bosniak side arguing that a significantly smaller people cannot be allotted the same number of ministers as the Bosniak people. So it's the same old story which resulted in the fact that instead of parity in the government, we now have disparity, and there's a situation in which Croats can be down-voted. That's the reason why the chamber of peoples in the federation often stops legislative initiatives, thus protecting the constituent quality of peoples. And this then hinders all activities. At the state level the Bosniaks are trying, just as I said when we were establishing the federation, I was a member of the first council of ministers that was established after Dayton, and after long debates and when the Serbs from the Republika Srpska started participating in the state structures and once a law was adopted for Bosnia-Herzegovina, a law full of compromise, there was resistance to the implementation or enforcement of these laws, because immediately after the publishing of the laws the Bosniak side wanted them to be amended and to the effect of go -- moving into the direction of a normal civil state, as they said, and this resulted in the construction on the part of the Serbs at state level and also on the part of the Croats, who felt that this was another step away from the parity brought about by Dayton. For example, when the first council of ministers was established, there were two co-presidents, a Serb and a Bosniak, and the -- a Croat was the vice-president. The Croat could never chair a session, but instead one week, the sessions would be chaired by a Serb and the other week by a Bosniak, a Muslim. What followed were the activities of the Bosniak side to change Dayton and to abolish the Republika Srpska, which certainly resulted in a mobilisation on the Serb political scene which rose to defend Dayton, and the present situation is the following: The Bosniaks still want to build a centralised state based on the principle of one man, one vote. The Serbs, fearing that the Republika Srpska could be abolished, are threatening that they will obstruct and no longer take part in the work of the authorities. So they are dissatisfied and in conflict with their partner, with their former partner in government, because the government was formed by a coalition of three parties. And the Croats are dissatisfied because they're part of a federation in which they feel they haven't resolved the issue they have always wanted to resolve based on the principle of equality. They now try to assert that at state level, but there -- there they come into conflict with the Bosniaks because -- who think that this is an issue to be dealt with and which is resolved at the level of the federation. So the situation is very difficult and complex, possibly the most problem-ridden ever since Dayton, because even after a series of change and reform-oriented legislation and financial help from the international community, the World Bank, the European Bank, the IMF, et cetera, but the political -- that political issue is the issue of all issues still.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tomic. You basically explained, I would say briefly explained this complex political situation. Can we then say that the issue of the position of each people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, bearing in mind the various views of the leaders of the Bosniak, Croatian, and Serbian peoples are still in existence the same way as they were in the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: To explain it to the Chamber, you mentioned the council of ministers several times. Under the Dayton Accord this was basically the government at state level, wasn't it, the only institution with executive powers?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the council of ministers became the state government after Dayton.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Let us now continue with the questions about financing. You explained to us during direct that these issues as feeding the budget or channeling the re -- the funds from the budget was being debated at government sessions. I will show you one of the -- some minutes from these sessions for you to say whether the problem was almost identical throughout 1993 or including the end of 1992. The document is P 00950. These are the minutes of the government session held on the 23rd. This is barely legible, but anyway, it was in December 1992. You were present at that session, weren't you? I'll refer to page 4 in the Croatian version at 10, and it's on page 7 of the English text. This is basically the first fully legible paragraph. The principle how funds were requested by some departments and how they were approved. The HVO HZ -- "At the proposal of the HVO HZ HB Defence Department a decision was issued unanimously setting aside. "The sum of 50.000 Croatian dinars ... "The sum of 30.000 Croatian dinars for assistance to the disabled." And now what follows: The sum of 90.000.000 Croatian dinars is to be set aside as an advance payment for the Defence and 15 million for the Department of the Interior, and at the end it says these funds will be paid out of the HZ HB budget until the end of the year. Can you please explain whether this was the principle of the distribution of funds based in 1992 and did you expect at the end of the year that possibly in the following year you will have the funds that you will be able to grant without down payments?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the end of the year. We started raising or collecting funds from customs and part of the taxes due to the poor functioning of the SDK. That's why I'm saying part of the funds, and that's when we started to allocate funds at the sessions of the HVO HZ HB in accordance with the resources available and in accordance with our estimates of what we would be able to raise by the end of the year, which was important for the department of defence and the department of the interior to be able to plan, because they were the most significant budget beneficiaries. And this -- that's why this reads that the funds will be paid out until the end of the year. Obviously we didn't have them at our disposal at that time. At that moment it was still too early to start thinking about a classical budget for 1993, but that's why we introduced the system I had mentioned earlier of monthly and quarterly plans for the departments to enable us to allocate the funds raised reduced in proportion or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I have another document, the minutes of the government session dealing with this. I believe that before the break I'll be able to complete that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before -- before we move to another document, I'd like to dwell on this one, because there is something that I find very interesting. Mr. Stojic takes the floor at some stage and said that the military courts are not functioning, and he explains that there are 1.000 police reports waiting to be dealt with and this is causing a problem in investigations. And he also referred to detentions, and of course there's also a problem there because there aren't any judicial decisions. Following Mr. Stojic's intervention, it seems that judges and prosecutors would be appointed, that's at the very end of the document, in order to try and address this situation. Of course appointing judges and prosecutors have financial implications, budgetary implications, and so on. So we are now in December 1992. It will take some time before all these people are appointed and before the system starts running again. According to you, was the system going to work again? And I'm talking specifically about military courts. In other words, during the year 1993 were you told of problems related to the fact that there weren't any prosecutors, that there weren't any judges, that there was no investigation, that there was no money? Were you told that there was a problem in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were informed by the heads of the defence department about the drafting and about the impossibility to punish those who had left their units or the battlefield because there was no judicial system in place. I believe that it was only during that month that we allocated some funds to the judicial department for the reconstruction of buildings, because in Mostar the buildings were badly damaged. There were no windowpanes, et cetera, and this was -- these funds were meant for the re-establishment of the judicial system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are saying that you made an effort, but my question is was it working or wasn't it working -- or wasn't it working, or wasn't it working properly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my opinion it was functioning poorly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is now 10.30. We need to have a break. We shall have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, with regard to the functioning of the judiciary that His Honour Judge Antonetti asked you, could you please confirm whether the reason for what you say that it never functioned properly, was one of the reasons the permanent persistent lack of funds in the justice system? You told us that the lack of funds was pervasive throughout the HVO system, but did this lack of funds reflect as one of the factors to the overall functioning of the judiciary?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphones are off for the witness. Could they please be switched on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Well, I have already said that some of the -- part of the jurisdiction of the budget of the HVO HZ HB was to fund the district courts, the district public prosecutors' offices, the municipality's financed municipal courts. Those municipal courts did not exist in each and every municipality before the war. Mostar was the centre in this context, I would say, and in Mostar there was a problem with the facilities that had to be reconstructed. Money was needed for that. There was the personnel problem, too, because lots of people left. The first to leave were the Serbs who had taken part in the judiciary. Most of them left, followed by many women who left together with their children and families as refugees. And also there was this issue of salaries, wages for those who worked there. It was a persistent issue when it came to providing conditions for the proper operation of the judiciary.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In addition to the wages was there also a problem of equipment and appropriate premises, adequate premises where judicial organs could work?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did mention that buildings had sustained damage, and the HVO HZ HB first provided assistance to the judiciary by funding the reconstruction of some of the facilities and also by providing money for the wages and also some basic texts and equipment such as computers.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now move on to the topic that we raised earlier. Could you please look at document P 01137. It is the next document in the Defence binder. These are the minutes from the meeting of the HVO HZ HB session of the 15th of January, 1993. I note here that you were not present at this meeting, but could you please look at page 3 in the Croatian version, item 6. That's at page 4 in the English version. We are talking about the very same things that you mentioned when you talked about the submission of the quarterly proposals. Let me just read this. I'm sure that you went through these minutes later. Do you perhaps recall of this development? It says here at the top of the page, page 3 in the Croatian version: "The draft financial plan of the Defence Department of the HVO HZ HB for the period from the 1st of January to the 31st of March, 1993, is submitted by the Defence Department of the HVO HZ HB. "Following a discussion of the said draft, the following conclusion was unanimously reached: "We must exert maximum efforts to ensure salaries for members of the armed forces and the settling of their material expenses." Mr. Tomic, does this fully confirm what you've told us about the quarterly plans, financial plans, and can we see from this that there still isn't enough funds because the conclusion states that maximum efforts must be made to ensure that those funds are obtained?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this conclusion was passed in accordance with the valid decree on the budget that funds should be planned for quarterly periods. The defence department did submit this request, and it was obvious that -- that this request could not be complied with. And in this context, this conclusion gives an incentive to make this effort to obtain the funds that could then be channeled into at least part of the salaries and material expenses of the personnel of the armed forces as indicated here in the conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could we now look at how this proceeded, what the financial situation was when it came to the financing of the defence effort. The next document is P 01324. These are the minutes from the HVO session. The date is the 27th of January, 1993. You attended this session. The page reference is 2 in the Croatian version, page 3 in the English version where it says, before the agenda is discussed, before item 1, it says: "Finally the head of the Defence Department, Mr. Stojic, asked the HVO of the HZ HB for assistance in materiel and technical equipment, particularly special purposes equipment, protection equipment, in addition to implementing the financial system as soon as possible so that the assistance could be realised." Mr. Tomic, we can see here that some 13 days later Mr. Stojic again presses the issue about implementing the financial system, making it operational, because it is obvious that there are some problems in terms of financing the defence. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let us look at the next document. That would be document 1D 01183. Yes, it's correct in the transcript. These are the minutes from the HVO session. The date is the 18th of March, 1993. Mr. Tomic, I picked and chose some, just some of the documents to make sure that these problems persisted throughout the year. So now we're in March. You were present at this session. Can we please look at -- we can see on the agenda under item 4: "Draft Decree on the protection of military persons with a military disability caused by the war at the time of an imminent threat of war or the state of war in the area of the HZ HB." This item is discussed at page 4 in the Croatian version, and it's page 2 in the English version. Could we now look at the procedure, how things were proposed by various departments. We can see that this draft decree on the protection of disabled war veterans when there is an imminent threat of war or a state of war in the area of the HZ HB, and there is also the draft decree on a one-off financial assistance. Both were submitted by the defence department. Mr. Bozic, Mr. Slobodan Bozic, notes that in accordance with the previous conclusion of the HZ HB HVO, drafts of the above-listed decrease have been composed, and an opinion on them must be sought from the finance department of the HZ HB HVO. And now we can see that in items A, B, C, and D Mr. Zubak proposes certain amendments. And then it goes on to say: "The decree on the protection of disabled war veterans and the decree on one-off financial assistance were adopted unanimously under the following conditions: The HZ HB HVO Defence department and the regulation commission of the HZ HB HVO should add legal and technical details to the decree in accordance with the above-listed objections. The date of implementation is the 1st of April, 1993." Let me now move on to the conclusion, and this is the conclusion of the HVO. "Organise and collect information on the payments made to members of the armed forces of the HZ HB on these reasons," and then it says that the decree shall be implemented on the 1st of April, 1993, and this will be done after information on the payments has been collected and recorded. And in item 3 the defence department, the department of the interior and the subdepartment of labour, social welfare and family are tasked with implementation of item 1. Mr. Tomic, is this a good example of the way in which the heads of departments proposed the draft laws or other legal instruments that the HVO had to finally pass? Was this how it was done? A draft is submitted, it is discussed, if there are any proposals or any remarks this is done, and then this is all reaffirmed in the conclusions. Can we say that this was the methodology how the proposals or drafts by certain department heads were actually adopted?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was the way that I described earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we then conclude, Mr. Tomic, that the heads of the departments or departments actually depended on the debate at the sessions of the HVO or, in other words, that each of their proposals, draft decrees or recommendations for personnel appointments were up for and that changes and demands could be made and that their drafts and proposals would then not be adopted in the way that they were tabled?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was this possibility. The head of a department tables an appointment or a draft decree at the session of the HVO where it is debated. If the majority is opposed, then the head of the department can decide to withdraw the document that was tabled or any other proposal, draft a new one or take on board the remarks or criticisms that were made, you can see that Mr. Zubak here dealt with some legal details, and incorporate them in the final version of the decision. And then after this is taken to the vote it becomes a document of the HVO HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The HVO could also make suggestions as to what needs to be amended, reaffirm this in the conclusion, conclusion and order that this be done in that manner; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could we please look at page -- at the last page just to confirm something about a document that Mr. Karnavas asked you about. We can see that item 11 at the last page of the minutes indicates that an amount of 5 million is set aside for the purposes of the Sarajevo HVO, the municipal HVO. For the transcript we saw the document 1D -- 1D 02114 allocating those found the Sarajevo HVO, and we can see that this was done at this session of the HVO. Let me ask you just one brief question regarding the Sarajevo HVO. At that time, from the time when the aggression against Sarajevo started up until the end of 1993, the HVO defended Sarajevo together with the BH army against the Serb aggressors, against the city itself and Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now I've moved on to October. Let me show you the document that was already shown to you by my colleague Mrs. Alaburic. That's document P 505799 [as interpreted]. P 0 -- let me repeat. P 05799. That's the minutes from a session of the HVO. The date is the 9th of October, 1993. The reason why I'm showing you this document, apart from the fact that you were present at this meeting, together with the document 1D 1934, let me remind you it's not in my binder but that's your letter, your report about the functioning of the financial system that you submit on the 12th of August, 1993. And Judge Trechsel asked you in this regard whether anything changed after this warning of yours, and you said that something did indeed change, and I will ask you to what extent, because I will -- in light of the fact that at this session on the 9th of October, 1993, now I'm talking about page 2 in the Croatian version, that would be page 3 in the English version, that's conclusion number 3 where the HVO passes a conclusion on the basis of the single financial system to ensure that payments are made into the budget in order to pay salaries to the troops in accordance with the standard criteria. Not a single state organ, public or other enterprise may start out paying salaries before the troops have received their salaries. I wanted us to -- I wanted you to tell us clearly how much things changed, objectively speaking, after this letter that you sent, because it appears to me that based on this document and other documents that followed that qualitatively speaking, no major changes occurred?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was yet another appeal or an attempt to exert pressure to ensure that the system would finally become operational. And as I said, through the 1994 budget, satisfactory steps were taken. Up until that time we're talking about makeshift solutions, one-upmanship with the municipalities that were trying to cover up funds that they had. And also they used funds in an improper manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, you said something quite interesting yesterday, that after some unfortunate events on the battlefield, militarily speaking, the municipalities would always try to keep the money for themselves and would try not to pay them into the budget of the HVO. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Was this yet another thing that affected the defence effort and affected negatively the effort to defend the parts of the HVO that were under attack?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We're about to conclude this topic. Let me just confirm what you said. That's document P 06689. This is a document sent to the presidents of the HVO by the president of the government. That's the 16th of November. The government of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna is already elected, and the prime minister, Mr. Prlic, states in the first passage -- I'm sure that you've seen this document. Appeals or urges the municipalities and the ministries to make this financial system operational because this was causing great problems to the government that had just been formed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me now move on to a different topic. Could you please look at document 2D 00891. It's a session of the HVO dated the 9th of April, 1993. You attended this meeting. I would now like to go through this with you to see how and what authority heads of the departments had within HVO. Page 8, first passage. That would be page 6, third paragraph in the English version. It says here: "At the proposal of the Defence department of the HVO unanimous decision was made about entering into contracts with the metal processing company Uzor in Siroki Brijeg about the manufacturing of the shells to be signed by the head of the defence department of the HZ Hb according to the prices and quantities listed in the contract." Do you remember such a conclusion being passed?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now I'm going to put questions to you in relation to the next document, 2D 00980. This is a decision on the conclusion of a contract with the mentioned company authorising the head of the defence department to conclude this contract. Mr. Tomic, on the basis of this one can see that the HVO in respect of such contracts gave authority to heads to sign contracts like this, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that this was an exception. At the proposal of the head of the defence department, because I think that it had to do with the first contract, and it was a privately owned company, too, so that was the reason why this proposal was made to make such a decision by the HVO HZ HB, because at that time there were -- there was no public procurement and there was no other way of dealing with things in a transparent fashion, especially in relation to private companies.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Before that, I would like to correct something on page 47, 18. The 2D 00980. That is the actual reference. And then I'm going to ask you when this system of public procurement and checking the system as such started operating.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was incorporated in the budget for 1994 as an obligation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tomic, during the direct examination you were shown a decision on the implementation of Article 25 of the law on customs and tariffs in the territory of the HZ HB at the time of an imminent threat of war and state of war, and that was a document that you are certainly familiar with. I did not put it in my binder. 1D 00019.
