In Article 4 of this decision it is stated that the armed forces of the HZ HB and the RBiH are exempt from paying customs duty on goods that are imported and that are used for the development of these services. So this tax exemption or customs exemption pertain to the army and -- of Bosnia-Herzegovina as well; right?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did this decision pertain to gasoline, crude oil, fuels? Were these the goods that were being imported?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, were they exempt from turnover tax in respect to these goods too?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Turnover tax follows the provisions of customs regulations. So if there was an exemption from customs duty, then the same applied for a turnover tax.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Were there gasoline stations in the HZ HB where fuel was provided for defence needs and was this recorded? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the gasoline stations were mobilised by the municipalities and for the most part these were formerly socially own, state-owned gasoline stations. And many units actually took fuel there by handing in appropriate documents that they had received from their own logistics people.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The managers of these gasoline stations, did they have to keep precise records as to how much fuel they issued for defence purposes so that they would be tax exempt and customs duty exempt for those quantities?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you remember that there was some abuse and that some gasoline stations pretended to have issued more fuel to the HVO precisely in order to dodge these tax obligations and customs duty obligations?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now let us look at document P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Nozica, I just note that you are leading, leading, leading, leading and this is not a different matter. It isn't the same line as the main interrogation and so it would be preferable if you could come back to open, more open questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps I did not realise that I was putting leading questions. I give the witness the possibility to explain what his knowledge is in respect of every one of my questions. I did not proof this witness, and of course I depend on the witness himself in terms of the progress I can make.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Have you found document P 01410? This is an order from Mr. Bruno Stojic showed several times here in the courtroom, and he is issuing Mr. Andabak an order to take over the complete business documentation of gasoline stations of Peric Ljubuski, Dodig-Citluk and Bosnjak Posusje, Dodig-Citluk and Bosnjak Posusje, in order to ensure payment of sales tax and in that way secure funds for financing units of the Croatian Defence Council. This document was submitted to you, I see down here. Do you remember anything in relation to this document? And then I'm going to show you further on the documents that relate to that.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember, of course, the entire situation in this regard, because practically this was a takeover of the powers of the finance department, because they were in charge of collecting turnover tax. However, these are three privately owned companies, gasoline stations, that is, that had not been mobilised. There was information and so on and so forth they were not paying all taxes, that they were handling this in a different way, and the municipal department of the municipalities of Ljubuski, Citluk, and Posusje had not established this. This is the period before the financial police was established. This point in time regulations had just been adopted and they -- the police started working in the first quarter of the year. After the documentation was compiled, certain reports were made. Finally this documentation was sent on to the financial police and the financial police dealt with these cases fully and they made decisions that were in accordance with the regulations prevailing in HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In relation to your question I'm going to put -- in relation to your answer I'm going to put a few questions to you. The records of fuel issued to the HVO, were they supposed to arrive to the defence department, to logistics there? Did they have to have records of all quantities that had been issued in order to see whether these were actually the quantities that were supposed to be issued in accordance with the orders?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the orders for taking over fuel were issued by the defence department or its services then that would have to go to the defence department to see what the situation was, to see what the documents issued were on the one hand and the fuel issued on the other hand. Practice showed and we had orders from municipalities that also made this possible, and for the most part this was not sent to the defence department of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me, please, if the defence department received information that some gasoline stations are showing larger quantities of fuel and that those that were in the original orders, were they duty bound to ask for a check of the work of these gasoline stations and the taxes paid?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. That was the procedure involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Would you tell me in this specific case the head of the defence department, did he actually carry out these checks or only if he received information that something irregular had happened, did he only ask for documentation then in order to establish what it was that was irregular, is this the gist of his order?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Finally that is its nature. These documents would ultimately be dealt with by the financial police of the HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Excellent. Let us look at another document now. Let us see if that is the document that would tally with what you said just now. That is the next document 2D 01475. This is a handwritten document, minutes. I don't know whether you remember it and whether you have ever seen it. Inopetrol Posusje, was that actually Bosniak Posusje?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The next one is circle Medjugorje. Is that Dodig-Citluk from that list?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And we also have Peric Ljubuski and that can be seen in the other document. This shows that the actual amount involved was 1.184.798 Deutschmarks that was paid or, rather, this much less. Do you remember that this was roughly the amount involved and do you remember that it was paid in subsequently?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the financial police dealt with this case file, and it was the meritorious institution because you see even the right names of the companies are not mentioned here but, rather, the surnames of the owners, whereas on this paper we see the actual names of the companies involved. Also, there's a remark down here circle Medjugorje duty to pay taxes on outgoing wholesale invoices to check against the invoices of the SDK. So this remark already says that this amount is not certain and it has to be checked against the invoices of the SDK of Mostar. The financial police dealt with the matter. They issued appropriate decisions, and they paid a certain amount. It was less than this, but it was a significant amount at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me, please, was this time also the time when the HVO had this chronical problem of financing? It has to do with the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. And this reaction of the defence department, that is how I understood it, was practically yet another attempt to ensure even more resources and to show on the other hand that there is an intensive search going on and that all methods would be resorted to in order to ensure resources for the budget of the HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like us to look at the next document. We finally have only two more documents to deal with, and this is a topic which indeed was not raised in the examination-in-chief and I am indeed in the hands of the Trial Chamber as to whether they are going to take this time away from my own time, and it has to do with procurement of weapons from Croatia and payments of these weapons and the other way around, having the HVO sell some weapons to Croatia. Mr. Tomic, I'm just going to make a brief introduction as to why I'm asking you this. The reason is that the indictment says that Croatia provided material assistance fully to the HVO HZ HB. There are documents that speak to the contrary, but in respect of this topic I'll just ask you briefly. Did you know, Mr. Tomic, that the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the very beginning the war in 1992, those who were living abroad, do you know whether they paid certain amounts of money for the defence of these areas and for the defence of Croatia? Could you briefly tell the Court whose citizens were working and living abroad for the most part? I'm referring to Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. And whose citizens paid the largest amounts of money? You said that at that time the system was not functioning, the payment system, so what accounts were used to have this money paid?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We saw in the decisions of the municipalities that they all went after a particular source of revenue and that is our workers who were temporarily employed abroad. Also through associations of citizens from their own municipality that existed throughout Europe and in America too. They asked for help, and Mostar had prepared this kind of a document asking for help. However, when we started working on the budget of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, we also thought that we could incorporate on the revenue side donations from our people, from the diaspora throughout the world who were calling and saying that they were willing to help their homeland. Most of the Croat -- Croatian diaspora is originally from Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, what was said then was that an agreement had been reached with Croatia that these resources should be centralised. So that people from municipalities and Herceg-Bosna and the Republic of Croatia would not turn to one and the same people and associations living abroad. So in that context we never planned for these resources in the budget as donations from the diaspora. These resources were allocated to a special account or to a multitude of accounts in banks in Austria and elsewhere, and these accounts were used by authorised persons from the Republic of Croatia. I know from the contacts that we had that Mr. Jozo Martinovic, who was at first the Minister of Finance in the government of the Republic of Croatia, that he was one of the signatories, and Mr. Susak, who was the minister for immigrants when this project started. Later on he became the minister of defence of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, even if these citizens wanted to make payments to banks in Mostar or in HZ HB, to banks there, did these banks function at all? Could they do it?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the Croatian bank DD in Mostar was established and its operations with foreign countries, it was impossible to make direct payments in the territory of HZ HB. That is to say one could use only an account in Croatia or in some other country.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you just tell us so that we could be as specific as possible, when was Hrvatska Banka, the Croatian bank established in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operations towards the end of 1992. The operations vis-a-vis foreign countries started towards the end of the first quarter of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, on the basis of what you've been saying so far, can I conclude that the resources that were coming from Croatia were in fact the money that was paid by citizens who originally hailed from Bosnia-Herzegovina, paid as their assistance the HVO? Can it be interpreted that way?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to object to that question unless there is a foundation for this witness being able to account for every dollar, every kuna or every dinar coming from [Realtime transcript read in error "to"] Croatia to [Realtime transcript read in error "from"] Bosnia. I don't really think he can do that, so I object to speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've taken note of your objection. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm done with this topic, and now I will ask you based on two documents how things functioned between Croatia and Herceg-Bosna. Let us look at document P 01511. These are the minutes of the 16th session held on the 18th of February, 1993. I'm referring to the conclusions on page 1 in the Croatian version. Actually, it's page 2, but they are both -- in the Croatian version they are both on one page. And in the English version. I don't know if you were present, but this reads: "The defence department of the HZ HB HVO is to make a request for the most essential goods from the Republic of Croatia through the HZ HB financial department in order to be reimbursed through the HZ HB Elektroprivreda and HEP." Mr. Tomic, if you read this conclusion by itself, it follows that HZ HB delivered electric power to Croatia and got something in return so that the electric power was not delivered for free.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This happened in the situation when the Elektroprivreda HZ HB had delivered power from the power plants Busko Blato and Capljina, and so the Croatian side had to pay for that. It is for -- it goes back to previous periods when power was delivered from the area of HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell us what HEP is?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: HEP is a Croatian -- the Croatian electric power company from Zagreb. And they agreed that some of their debts toward the -- would be paid to the HVO HZ HB through the delivery of goods of Croatian producers. Those are mostly meat products by Pik Vrbovec and other goods produced in Croatia. As the finance department needed to account for that compensation between HEP and Elektroprivreda as well as HVO HZ HB, this was a request to submit a list of products that we could send to the Croatian side, that is HEP, so that they could make us an offer for this compensation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, just to interrupt and for what it's worth but I would like the record to be as accurate as possible, I don't know if I misspoke or if it was a question of translation, but in any event it's left the page now but on page 55 of the transcript today at line 24 and 25, when I stated my objection, what I meant -- what I intended to say, whether I said it or not I don't know, but every kuna or every dollar coming to -- it's recorded in the transcript as coming to Croatia from Bosnia and what I certainly intended to say if I did not was every kuna or every dinar coming to Bosnia from Croatia. Just so the record's clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now that the transcript has been corrected, we can move to the next document. Please take a look at document 2D 01476. Can you remember anything -- and I'll try to remind you. This is an invoice dated 15th of April, 1993, submitted by the defence department and its head Bruno Stojic to the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, the provision, procurement and production department, based on a contract dated December 10th, 1992, and it follows from this invoice that the HVO or the defence department is selling to the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia a land cannon with spare parts, tools and an accessory kit as well as an aircraft cannon with spare parts, tools, and an accessory kit. The prices are set here. They amount to a total of 471.460 Deutschmarks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Nozica --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not extremely important but I think it's three cannons and two aircraft cannons and not one each, if you look at the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree. It's about three land cannon and two aircraft cannon. I failed to say that but it is obvious from the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, can you remember anything regarding this document?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The defence department, like all budget beneficiaries, could generate some own revenue. For that revenue -- that revenue was part of the report on the financial aspect of the budget that is submitted to the -- submitted at the end of the year so that the finance department could not directly see how this revenue is generated except for the total sums that were mentioned in the relevant documents in their total value. And these were the amounts that were part in the annual reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, I'm not showing this document to you only to show how much revenue was generated in this way. I would like to know why this came about. First to see that the -- there was a business relation between -- in place and to show that the HVO, having drafted this contract on the 10th of December, 1992, is giving some of its equipment to Croatia from which we can conclude whether or not they are preparing for an offensive in the war. Can you -- do you agree with me that we can conclude as much from this document with regard also to the information that you had about this revenue having arrived to the defence department?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. This concludes my interrogation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I? I would like to ask one or two more questions. You were asked whether you were aware of this transaction and your answer was rather general. Were you aware, do you remember this transaction, these five guns?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember that concrete transaction from the time it took place, but it was mentioned in the financial report of the defence department for the year 1993, and it is part of the own revenue, a chapter of their overall revenues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I would be interested to know what kind of guns these were and where they came from. Were they produced within the area of HZ HB? Were they used material? Were they new? Can you tell us anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I cannot say much about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you permit, we will have a Defence witness, Mr. Stojic, who will explain what kind of cannon this is about. We only asked the witness what he was in a position to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That's perfectly all right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tomic, I'd like to ask you a much more general question on the basis of this document. This document shows a link between the HVO and the Republic of Croatia. However, my question is focused on the relationship from the Republic of Croatia to HVO on the financial aspects of things. To your knowledge did the Republic of Croatia grant loans, whether official or not, to the HZ HB at that time? Regular loans with documents? I could give you examples. For instance, a loan in 1998 between the Islamic Republic of Mauritania and an African development fund. So these things happen in international law. You can have loans between states and other states or between states and institutions. So to your knowledge did financial links exist between the Republic of Croatia and the HZ HB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No contractual relationship existed between the Republic of Croatia and the HZ HB. There was financial aid based on the funds raised from the diaspora. Those accounts, as I said, were in Austria and other countries where that money was remitted. The people who were authorised to manage those accounts did not channel that aid to the HZ HB. That aid came from other sources, and the money that was on foreign accounts in convertible currency was used for the defence of the Republic of Croatia. For example, I've already said that at the moment when the accounts were opened Mr. Martinovic was Minister of Finance and Mr. Susak was the minister of emigres. They went to foreign countries and lobbied among the Croatian emigres to send money. And it went through these two persons, not institutions. Mr. Susak later became the minister of defence of the Republic of Croatia, but his activity was that of a signatory of an account opened in Filah [phoen] or other places where these accounts were. Mr. Martinovic, after, when he was no longer Minister of Finance went to the Privredna Banka where he had come from also and was in the position to influence the use of those resources, and if he would sign an order for a certain amount in Croatian dinars as aid, the Privredna Banka Zagreb --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, the interpreters cannot follow. Could the witness repeat once more slowly, more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps he could repeat the last part of the answer. It was very clear that at some point the translation stopped. So if you could go a little slower.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. It's about that part when Mr. Martinovic, when he ceased to be minister went to the Privredna Banka Zagreb, and he still remain a signatory together with Mr. Susak, authorised to withdraw money from that account. And the transfers that came to that account for any reason, and the reason must be stated for a transfer to be effected, the -- they used the resources at their disposal such as the interest payable on the part of the Privredna Banka. And those amounts in Croatian dinars were then forward as aid to the HZ HB, and the Privredna Banka, instead of buying foreign currency in the market, would simply cover that amount from the account in Filah. So that -- in other words, that was a compensation of the -- the amounts that they had remitted and which stemmed from the donations of emigre Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the budget of the HZ HB is concerned I assume there were documents relating to the budget which all and everyone can see, and that I'm -- in these documents I'm sure we can see revenues and expenses columns. And if there were revenues that were -- did not come from the budget, this would be mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you transfer budget items to other budget items? For instance, amounts that were allocated to a particular budget item for X, Y, Z reason, you would reallocate those amounts to other items. Did that ever happen? What I mean is perhaps defence items.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must say that for 1992 and 1993 there was no real budget in the sense you are using the word. The budget was only formed for 1994. And when a reallocation of funds was necessary that exceeded the planned amounts by 10 per cent or more, the budget had to be rebalanced, especially if the amounts from the current reserve of the budget are not sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm now turning to other Defence counsel. I don't know how much time you have had so far, two hours, perhaps. I'm about to tell you. Two hours and 26 minutes. One hour 17 minutes for the first Defence team and one hour 19 minutes for the second Defence team. Ideally we should be able to finish today so that the Prosecution can start its cross-examination next week. That said, this will be very tight. I hope there won't be too many objections. I had hoped we could be sitting on Wednesday, but that will not be the case. We will only be able to have a hearing on Monday and Tuesday, which will make it very short. At 1.00 on Tuesday there's a Plenary Session for the Judges to elect the president and adopt two articles amending the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. I hope that this will be finished by a quarter past 2.00. As far as I'm concerned, I will be standing at the door at 14 minutes past 2.00. So what is it to be?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. As far as I know, it's only the General Praljak Defence that will be cross-examining this witness, so I expect that we will not have to go beyond today. The cross-examination by General Praljak's Defence will pertain to the answers the witness gave in the examination-in-chief at pages 33707, lines 16 through 24; 33708, line 18 through 25; 33709, lines 22 through 25; 33713, 33714, 33738. Those are the pages in the transcript. The date is the 27th of October. So the first day of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Tomic. Let us go back to 1992 to Mostar to the situation that prevailed in Mostar in early -- let's say up until mid-1992. I would like to ask you to look at document 1D 00909 which is in the small binder that you have in front of you. I will now ask you whether you were aware or whether you knew Mr. Slobodan Lang, Dr. Slobodan Lang.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to meet with Dr. Lang?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us when?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- well, we first met in May in Mostar. I think it was the logistics centre that was set up in the basement of a building in Mostar. The building was called Lesnina, and that's where I met Mr. Lang, who told us about his experience from Dubrovnik, and that's what stuck in my mind. That's why I remember his visit to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like you to look at this document, which is entitled the "Drama of Mostar, the 9th and the 10th of May 1992." It is signed by Dr. Lang, among other signatories, and I would like to ask you this: Do you recall this claim and can you confirm it that all the barrels were trained on the town on the 9th of May and that the town was encircled? I mean Mostar.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: You mentioned this, but would you agree with me that about 65 per cent of the civilians had left Mostar at that time?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Can you confirm that the civilian structure that had been inherited from the previous system either did not exist or was not functioning, was in disarray?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Is it true -- is it true that on the 7th of May the town was completely cut off in terms of telecommunications? 1992, yes. I'm talking about 1992.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that this was in early May, and I assume that the date is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: At that time that we're talking about in May?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in early May.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, the speakers are kindly asked not to overlap.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: It says here and I don't know if you can remember that, but at any rate, that in the afternoon on the 9th an artillery attack was launched on Mostar and that it last for almost 24 hours and that several thousand shells were fired. Do you recall that, the atmosphere, the situation, the shelling of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember the situation. Now, whether it was on the 9th or the 10th, I can't really play that back in my mind, but I do remember this action that is described here, an attempt to launch a tank attack from the south. And I remember that the HVO members repelled the tank attack, and I know that it was about that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. As you go through this document were you able to read the other claims about the ambulances that were no longer there, about the burial of those who had been killed in the Liska park?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, one of my family members was buried in the Liska park because it was impossible to carry out the regular funeral.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: So can you confirm that the claims made in this letter or report by Dr. Lang tally with what you experienced, saw, went through?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to apologise, I haven't read this through. But up until the middle of page 2 it reflects in its entirety the atmosphere as it prevailed in Mostar. I can go on to the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I have not seen this document before. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: So you can confirm.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does correspond with the situation as it was in Mostar at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have only one question for you, and then with the permission of the Trial Chamber General Praljak would like to talk to you about the year 1992 and the situation in Mostar and the events in Mostar and in Hercegovina. Let me just ask you this: Do you know who Radoslav Zovko is? Have you heard of him?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that Radoslav Zovko -- I think there was a friar or a priest, his name was Radoslav Zovko.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Have you heard about the "Mostarski Dnevnik," the "Mostar Diary"?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, with your permission General Praljak would like to continue the cross-examination of this witness regarding the situation in Mostar and in Herzegovina in 1992 about the events in which he himself took part and has direct knowledge of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, before I give the floor to General Praljak, I have a few questions based on this document. These events occurred on the 9th and 10th of May, 1992. Sixty-five per cent of the population, according to this document, this amounts to 70.000 people, left Mostar. These people who left Mostar, I assume among those people there were both Croats, Muslims and maybe Serbs. Did some of these people come back again or did they leave for good?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this exodus all people left because they wanted to take care of their families. The male members of the family would put their families up in some hotel or with their families in Western Herzegovina, Croatia, or wherever further afield, would -- and then they would go back in order to try and protect their property, houses, apartments, to be there and to take part in the defence. And then as operations in Mostar after the liberation from the JNA and the reservists subsided, some of the family members came back but then they left again when the conflict broke out between Croats and Muslims in Mostar. Nowadays in Mostar, the bottom line, to use the financial term, is that today most of the people who had come back are Croats. A part of Bosniaks had come back and some of the Serbs had also come back. As far as the residents of the city itself, the urban population, for the most part Muslims went back to Sarajevo, not to Mostar because they couldn't find their way around in the new circumstances. Some of my best friends who were Bosniaks preferred to go back to Sarajevo instead of Mostar because Mostar has suffered a huge influx of rural population that imposed their values. The refugees had come in from all over Bosnia from rural areas, and they enjoyed the status of war heroes and they had a negative attitude towards the return of the original residents of Mostar, and that's why most of them decided not to come back to Mostar but to go to Sarajevo. As far as Serbs are concerned, lots of Serbs, the urban Serbs from Mostar, remained in Belgrade. Some of them remained in Trebinje. As for Croats from the urban population, quite a few of them remained in Zagreb or in Split.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I notice that from Hum, Orlovac, and "forteca," the Hum hill, I mean, shots were fired, and according to the document religious buildings were hit in the process, dioceses, cathedrals, churches. As far as you know, the shelling by the Serb artillery, do you know whether they damaged any mosques?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: All the mosques or some mosques? Since you were the mayor of Mostar in the year 2000, you know this town pretty well. Maybe you could tell us whether all the mosques were hit or just a few mosques?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time I participated together with my colleagues in Mostar writing a book about the urbicide in Mostar and there was an exhibition in Split as part of our effort to collect aid, and in this document you can see the images of the damage caused to all public buildings in Mostar, and I think that most of the mosques had been hit. The minarets were torn down on some of them or had suffered damage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were an author to this book "Urbicide," were you? This is a book we have seen already. I see that this document talks about the Old Bridge, which is the crux of the matter for this Trial Chamber. When the Serbs fired shots, as far as you know do you know whether the Old Bridge was damaged? I don't mean destroyed, because it didn't fall in 1992, but was it slightly damaged, seriously damaged, only damaged in part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there was some damage, and I remember that timber and tyres, car tyres, were used to protect the bridge from further targeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question, and I believe my colleague would like to put questions to you also. I can see in this document that the authors of this document, Mr. Slobodan Lang, talks about the press and seems to indicate, at any rate, in May 1992 that -- that no foreign journalist, be he or she, Bosniak or a Croat, on the spot in paragraph 2. So it seems that nobody could recount what had happened. Was that the feeling you had also, that the international press or national press had not been allowed in and was not present when the shelling occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's my impression. And one of the first projects that we had in the Special Purpose Council was to procure equipment for the Mostar radio station that we obtained through a donation by a company from Croatia. And after this station was set up you could at least hear the reports from Mostar that could then be rebroadcast by others, because in Mostar the media were just not present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, my question was initially a twofold question, but the Presiding Judge has put the first part of the question. I'd like to get back to the 9th and the 10th of May. The document says that it's really dramatic for Mostar, the events that are described here, and that this is really and truly dramatic. The artillery started shelling on the 9th and only stopped shelling four hours later. We have heard a lot of witnesses in this court stating that the JNA was one of the most powerful armies in the world with extremely well-trained officers, well-versed in the laws of war and humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Humanitarian law issues, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand correctly, the JNA had essentially targeted civilian, medical, religious and cultural buildings, amongst others, the Old Bridge. The problem I have here is the terms used, "essentially targeted." Do you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whatever was destroyed was designated the key target, because if something was targeted -- if something was hit and destroyed, then obviously it was a target, and since practically all the public buildings were hit, then that was the conclusion, that they were indeed the main target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because during a war there is what is called collateral damage. Would the civilian buildings be considered part of this collateral damage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know there were no military operations launched from the town itself. There were no major gun emplacements, artillery pieces that were fired, no resistance was offered from those buildings by, for instance, firing those cannon. And then the JNA -- then you could say that the JNA's returning fire and destroying those gun emplacements. That was not the case. They were firing on the civilian targets in order to exert pressure on the civilian population to make them flee the city in as large numbers as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There it is. That was my question, what was the purpose of this operation, but you have already answered this question. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems, looking at the document, this is -- is in the part of the document which mentioned the 9th and the 10th of May. It seems that the Serbs lost three of their tanks. Does this mean that there was fighting between the Serbs and the forces opposing the Serbs since I see here that three tanks are mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it involves the attack that I mentioned that I know happen at that time when they set off with armoured vehicles from the south along the Bulevar, that is to say the street going through the middle of town. On the south they were stopped by the members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. My last question and we will have the break afterwards and Mr. Praljak can take the floor after the break. He will have ample time to put his questions. The question I would like to put to you has to do with the media. We can see that there were no journalists there. This is what this document states. In the following months, apart from the radio stations were the media able to cover any of these events, and if that was the case, who was writing about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in the later stage, except for Radio Mostar, another radio station started operating in the eastern part of town, that is to say after the conflict between the Bosniaks and the Croats. For the most part it involved bulletins, if I can put it that way, of individual units. That is to say there weren't any printed newspapers or periodicals from the area of the HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. We shall have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. The Court will give the floor to Mr. Praljak, and we will like to say that Mr. Praljak is allowed to ask questions along as they relate to his area of expertise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Tomic. Do you know me from earlier on? Yes?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please look at 3D 03096. This is the "Mostar Diary" of Mr. Radoslav Zovko. I'll try move on as fast as possible without overlapping, though, because I have to refer to individual pages. And the diary has to do with the first half of 1992 in Herzegovina and Mostar. At that time you were in Mostar; right?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In order to be as brief as possible, I'm going to make a reference in Croatian to the page number. Please look at page 36. Friday, the 10th of January, 1992, the attack on the train in Mostar. It says: "Two railway workers were wounded, one Muslim, one Croat, because reservists opened fire at a freight train." As you were there day in, day out, did you know about this?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let's look at the next page, that is page 39 of the Croatian book. On the 24th of January, 1992, a referendum was voted for in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Assembly was in session, and the main problem was to have a referendum for an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina, it says the Serbs blocked the work of the Assembly by leaving it and today they're doing it by filibustering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, we have a little problem. We are also a little delayed because you only give the number of the Croatian version, which means that then we must look at what date you speak about and then we must try to find this in the English version, and the first entry you have mentioned, 9th of January, does not figure in the translation, so we are a bit lost. The second, neither. Ours starts with the 25th of January. Well, it says "Attack on train," but we don't have the date. And then 24 January, we don't have.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to read the date, although you don't have it, but also read the heading like "Referendum voted for in Bosnia-Herzegovina" so then you will know what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And it says further on: "Nevertheless, after midnight the Serb delegates withdrew and the Assembly continued working normally. Decision on having a referendum was made." Are you aware of this fact, these endless sessions of the Assembly, the obstruction by the Serbs and so on?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: "Hunger knocking at the door," right underneath. The 25th of January, 1992. It says here that the Yugo dinar was depreciated again by 400 per cent. And then there is a reference to salaries, and finally it says: "Many of our young men joined the Croatian army or the police for patriotic reasons but also for the money, because life here is hard." Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: We'll see later on what Mr. Zovko says in terms of what the value of these different currencies are. For example, these salaries of about 5.000 Yugo dinars, was that approximately about 50 Deutschmark? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was it roughly in that period. One Deutschmark, 65 Yugo dinars. That would be it approximately.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Page 41. "Caritas in action." That is the 28th of January, 1992. It says the diocese and Caritas in Mostar is working at full steam. There are a lot of paupers and people on the brink of poverty." Further on Zovko says: "Quite honestly perhaps there may be among them some who are feigning or maybe smuggling, but it's difficult to sort it out all the time." It also says there is problems in the distribution of food because some friars are running their own separate charities, they don't want to join the central one because it wouldn't be right if everything were all right. And then he makes a reference here to Mr. Zovko and then also that there was quite a bit of hunger in Mostar right then and also that there was this problem of these private Caritases run by individuals.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were queues, people queueing up for food.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: The next document is right down here, that is the 31st of January, 1992. It says: "Who is guarding what?" And it says that the reservists are holding both barracks, both airports and that they took control of the Austrian bunkers and fortresses on Velez and its slopes, Hum Orlovac and they're roaming the hill around Miljkovici and Krivodol. Did you know that, that already then actually the reservists had taken all the hills around Mostar?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Page 42, let's have a look at that. Cannons at Hum, the 3rd of February 1992, it says the reservists have rolled out tanks onto Hum and the surrounding hills. Their intention is obvious on the basis of what happened to Ravno. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the tanks -- or rather the tanks and cannons were on Hum and in Podvelezje and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let's move on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I'm sorry, it seems that we are hearing the testimony of Mr. Zovko. If fact, we have a witness here who is a special in finance matters and you put to him a diary of someone of whom we know not much. He may have an acute memory or not. He may be putting down what happens. It may all be true, but I do not quite see what the Chamber gains by the witness saying yes to what you read to us. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, please, please. Your Honour Judge Trechsel, first of all this man here is a man who lived through the experience and destiny of Mostar. The fact that you want him to be a financial expert only, that may be your wish, but my wish is to ask this man some questions. He had to take his family out of Mostar because of the terror that reigned there. He also buried a family member at the cemetery there, and he is not just an expert witness in finance. He is first and foremost a man who took part in all of this, and he is familiar with what is being avoided for months now in this court, and that is where all of this is taking place, all of this that we are discussing in the field of finance. What is happening is a brutal aggression which is clearly depicted here in an all-embracing and comprehensive way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, please allow me, Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The bench regulates --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- the proceedings here and neither the Prosecution nor the Defence nor the accused nor the witness. It is only the Bench who is in charge. I mean, you are just reading a book and the witness says yes, yes, yes. We've had that before, and we have said many times, not only me, that we do not gain much. If you want to ask him questions, ask him questions and prompt him to speak of his experience and not just to -- to nod to an experience someone else has put down in a diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you asked Mr. Praljak about the reasons why he is referring to that and he has stated those reasons. I just want to add a procedural --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have not asked --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, I will go back to that. I wish to refer to a procedural reason. According to the instructions issued by this Trial Chamber, there is a mechanism in place for adducing evidence. The Defence believes that this book is a relevant piece of evidence, proof of the situation in Mostar in 1992. The witness knows about this because he was there at the time. We are checking this document. We are trying to establish its authenticity. Tomorrow through the so-called IC list we are going to tender this document into evidence. Why? Because the Defence can present its arguments in the final brief that -- to the effect that what this witness has been speaking about and other witnesses, too, all of that happened within a particular context. To put it in simple terms, the HZ HB tried to establish civilian order at the time when chaos prevailed in town. You don't know that. You haven't seen that. You have only heard parts and pieces of that. We are trying to make a synthesis there. There is no better evidence than this kind of book like a diary. It is a live person who wrote this and now we have a live witness, a man who was there and who can confirm whether this corresponds to his knowledge. If it does correspond to his knowledge, then obviously this is authentic evidence. That's the core of the matter, and I believe that it is relevant to establish whether the HZ HB -- or, rather, the HVO HZ HB functioned in lab conditions, in a septic atmosphere, or in a real-life situation or, rather, the chaos of war. In conclusion, I have to say please look at the conclusion. Look at the incriminations in the indictment, the conduct of the so-called members of the JCE, specifically the HVO HZ HB from the 1st of September, 1991, and already by now we have seen through the evidence that in 1992 nothing happened in relation to the Muslims who are depicted as victims in the indictment. So that was not there. We have to show that 1992 is not a relevant year in the indictment in respect of the way it has been portrayed in the indictment. It is for you to assess the evidence, the Trial Chamber, but we are duty-bound as the Defence to present this kind of evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, please continue, but you're not going to review every single entry in the document, I hope. Just take a few examples and then ask brief questions to the witness and that will help to provide the witness longer answers maybe.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I understand that procedure is an essential part of the legal system, but at least ten times so far, I have tried to show what Mostar was like after the destruction inflicted by the Yugoslav People's Army and the reservists -- reservists. When I tried to introduce as evidence a book, you refused that. And I am now trying to hear from the witness whether he has read these pages and whether to the best of his knowledge by virtue of his having lived there he can corroborate that this is true. And I will be contented if this is admitted as evidence, because this is about the most essential things in the whole war, what is being avoided here in this court, namely desperation, fear, hunger, exhaustion, chaos, misery, et cetera. These were the conditions under which I and everybody else sitting with me here functioned, and this is an essential element which is currently being swept aside, and a case is built upon the assumption that there was a state in place, that there was peacetime, et cetera. If you let me, I will be -- I'll finish in four minutes. I was down there, and I can testify, but you give me 54 hours and the war lasted two and a half years. I cannot -- without witnesses I cannot explain the truth based on facts. So please allow me either to ask for four or five questions from here or globally to ask the witness how many aeroplanes flew over those areas, how many women and children they killed. I'm asking for instructions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of the book you can say the following to the witness: This diary describes a series of events on specific dates. I will take four or five examples of such events, and then you can talk about what happened on the 8th of April, 1992, or what happened on another day. Then he can confirm whether the events actually took place, and when he has then you can ask him another question and say, "Do you share such-and-such point of view?"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will obey.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So, Witness, a book has been presented to you, I hope that you have seen it before, from which I submitted to you some excerpts up until the 19th of June, 1992, which is on page 94, the last page, and I'm going to ask you a few more questions, something that has nothing to do with the facts that are only on paper. Page 42, "Roadblock at Balinovac." The --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot find the relevant passage.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the interpreters have lost track. The interpreters do not know where you are reading from and they stopped translating.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to page 42. The date is 4th of February, 1992. "Blockade at Balinovac."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Zovko says the following: "People have grown so sick and tired of this tension with the reservists. They almost don't care any more if a war starts. They just want this tension and uncertainty to come to an end." Witness, tell the Bench about the psychological situation prevailing in Mostar with regards to the activities of the reservists of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation was chaotic. The people were under pressure because on the surrounding hills heavy armaments were deployed. Reservists were roaming the town in their vehicles, and they were -- they went to inns and pubs and initiated conflict. They were firing from their weapons. People were coming out of their houses and buildings, gathered on the streets, and it was highly charged, the situation was highly charged. Prices rose at a breathtaking pace. There was ever-less merchandise and the prospect of people being paid for their work were getting slim. On the other hand, the reservists were receiving their salaries from the JNA and with freshly printed money they would buy the last goods available in Mostar, and the merchants could not renew their stock with Yugoslav dinars. The overall atmosphere was full of uncertainty and depressing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Page 43 in the Croatian text. "No petrol again. Another petrol crisis, none to be had by ordinary people while some are getting it due to their connections." And then it reads that 1 Deutschmark corresponds to 85 Yugoslav dinars. Was that really so?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The exchange rate deteriorated all the time and there was daily inflation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please go to page 50 of the Croatian version. The 5th of March, a Thursday. It reads: "Situation calmer." This now reads 1 Deutschmarks corresponds to 150 Yugo dinars. We can see inflation isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Below that, the next heading "Bozo Lasta killed in Tasovcici. At 2200 hours at the Capljina bridge one Bozo Lasta was killed gratuitously." Do you know there have been some incidents where people were killed by paramilitary forces without any reason, so drunken, reservists would kill someone?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have already said that there was much shooting and there were victims. And an even greater problem was inadequate information, and for that reason a snowball effect was created. So -- which resulted in much psychological tension among the citizens.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please go to page 53. It says: "Friday, 20th of March." The heading is: "The Chetniks are surprised. The Chetniks seem to have learned that in Croatia they just need to open fire a little and the people will flee. However, no one is fleeing from Jasenica, Rodoc and Krivodol." Is it true that the people were not so easily frightened and that they resisted the aggression by using weapons they had mostly procured themselves?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: The next heading reads "Provocations." In the night of the 20th of March -- of the 20th and 21st of March, the JNA strafed the little chapel at the Miljkovici cemetery and et cetera. I believe that you know these details?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with the incident at Miljkovici which is in the Mostar municipality and I heard the rest from the information that was around at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And it says further on that the -- under the next heading the Serbs have continued to shell Hrasno and environs, people are feeling from -- towards Stolac and Capljina, as it was. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Chapter -- or, rather, page 57. We're talking about the 4th of April, 1992. Near Tepa in Mostar a Muslim baker was killed yesterday, shot dead with five bullets for no reason at all. You witnessed that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Then there is the 7th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may add a question. What does it mean, Mr. Tomic, that you witnessed this killing of a baker?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Are you forbidding me to ask questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No. No. [Interpretation] I would just like to suggest that the transcript did not accurately record -- record the answer of the witness. The witness said yes, I witnessed such incidents and not that incident, and therefore it is logical that you asked your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. Can you then tell a killing that you actually witnessed, where you saw someone being killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not say that I saw that killing, but -- but that such things were happening at the time. I was informed of that, because I lived in Mostar at the time. My office was 200 metres away from the spot where that baker was killed, and that's why I remember that there was such an incident, but I was not present when -- when the man was killed, and I never testified about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. That -- that's a bit technical, you see, that we use the word witness, hearsay witness, things like that. Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Below that you will find that Alija Izetbegovic proclaimed a general mobilisation at Herceg-Bosna, did that this morning. Did you know that general mobilisation was declared and that the aggressor was named?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that -- that happened in this period.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please go to page 58, the 7th of April, 1992. The night of the 6th to the 7th of April was a real night of war in Mostar. From the north and south camps, the VJ kept Orlovac and Jasenica under barrage of fire. Croatia recognised BiH and granted double citizenship to the Croats in BiH. Early this morning at 6 hours 22, VJ MiGs attacked Listica. Six persons were killed. Citluk was also attacked from the air but I don't know if there were casualties. Listica is Siroki Brijeg, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know -- there is a series of such things in these texts? But do you know that the VJ MiGs regularly bombed Siroki Brijeg, Citluk, Livno, and Grude, in such a manner as to kill women, children, elderly people in areas where there were no armed forces and no resistance?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the time the aviation of the Yugoslav People's Army was active at the time. When we drove to Herzegovina via Makarska we drove without headlights so as not to attract their attention. We were advised not to put on our -- our headlights.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now we are moving to the 9th of April on page 60. This is very important. "Last night in Mostar was filled with gunfire. From the airport the VJ fired at Ljuti Dolac, Slipcici, and Krusevo with a multiple rocket launcher." And then the underlined part. "Our commander Perko ordered a retreat of our troops via Goranci. The troops saw that as treason, refused to obey the order and stayed in town, resisting the VJ."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down for the sake of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Perak [as interpreted] was a former officer of the Yugoslav People's Army who later on fled to Serbia and obviously he was placed there to issue the order to abandon Mostar and thus abandoning both the military and the civilians? Do you know of that?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that, especially after this refusal to obey the order and after they left the town I can confirm that this was indeed correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let us now move on to the 13th of April, 1992. That's at page 62. "Capljina and Livno under attack. The Yugoslav army is attacking Slipcici, Citluk, and in Bosnia Visegrad. And then it says from -- starting at 1525 hours the VJ attacked Capljina with a barrage of fierce artillery fire. The town is ablaze. Mogorjelo Hotel, the church, the mosque and many other buildings have been damaged. Jasenica is on fire. The army is either arresting or killing our people around town and the surrounding villages. Pavo Gagro was found at Buna with his throat slit." This tallies with the information that you provided earlier; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Pavo Gagro was the father of some well-known businessman in Mostar. I knew them through my work in the revenues department, and I remember this when he was found with his throat slit. Allegedly it was determined later that his neighbour, a Serb, actually murdered him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Fine. Let's see what else we'll find. Easter, 19th of April, 1992. That's at page 66. "Perisic is destroying Mostar."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, Mr. Praljak is kindly asked to give the interpreters some time to find the actual reference and then read slowly for the purpose of correct interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: "A pilot called and said that he had been abducted but then he went back --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, we really did cannot find this text.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: "At 1700 hours a pilot who had been abducted called from Sarajevo saying that he had deserted the Yugoslav People's Army, but Perisic continues with fierce artillery fire against Mostar, because this is not about the abducted pilots, his aim is to take control of Mostar. From Juzni Logor they fired at the bridge, the Hasan Brkica bridge. There were dead and wounded passers-by. Perisic completed his crime against Mostar at 2020 hours. We did not celebrate the whole evening mass and Easter because nobody had come on account of the shooting." Sir, was this the situation in Mostar throughout those months? And we will go through some other entries so throughout those months.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall this Easter, because as I said in my previous testimony when the tank truck exploded I organised for my parents to take my sister's children and my daughter to Makarska. Two weeks later my wife who remained in Mostar, and myself, we went there to visit them because it was Easter, for Easter holidays, and we went taking the only route that was still usable, the Gorancik route through Goranci. It was constantly exposed to fire from the artillery piece on the Hum hill. After Easter we wanted to go back to Mostar because my wife also wanted to go back to town. We came to Goranci, the village above Mostar, and at that time the last entry point where one could get into Mostar and out of Mostar was closed because of the shelling. We remained there almost a whole night waiting, and that's when I took my wife back to Makarska and she remain there with the children while I went back to Mostar again at night using the Goranci road during a lull in the shooting. So this was the atmosphere that prevailed in Mostar at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: At page 66 again, the 21st of April, "Eight hours of fighting. Hum was hit. He says in Mostar they are mopping up snipers and rumour has it that they include Muslims and Croats who are committing these crimes for money." Do you know that in the chaos and fear that reigned there were snipers operating and that it took a lot of work to catch some of them, and some of them were killed? There was looting, robbery, and Fra Zovko, Friar Zovko lists all that. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I know that in particular in Centar 2 that neighbourhood, it's a residential neighbourhood with a lot of apartment buildings, that snipers were active there as is described here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: As regards this road, the only one that was still in use and what it looked like, at page 67 Friar Zovko left town and he says: "I got out of Mostar." That's the entry. And he says: "I drove along the Goranac road, I was on top of Cim and nobody was shooting. I said the prayer of contrition several times." He talks about fence -- fences broken down, damage to the road, and he says, "I'm driving. I step on the gas." And he says, "I hope for a death more than for life." Coming from a priest, does that tell you what kind of a psycho-social situation the people were in in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that road, I mentioned it, I said that I used it too. The well-known Goranac dog leg is a very well-known place. It's such a sharp curve that you have to slow down to 20 kilometres per hour in order to get through it and this dog leg bend was constantly exposed to an anti-aircraft gun firing from Mount Hum. And this was really Russian Roulette. You didn't know whether you'd be able to get out of there. And the people who used the road drove too fast and accidents happened. People got killed either in accidents or because of shells. So taking that road was a gamble. And I understand what he means when he says that he's hoping for death more than for life.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, we will we have a major point at page 69, the 27th of April 1992, "a new so-called Yugoslavia." It says: "At 1300 hours the town of Mostar, Ilici and Cim came under heavy gunfire. At 1400 hours VBR fired at Krusevo, Biograci and Jare." And then at the end of this passage Friar Zovko says this and I'm going to ask you this: "There is a lot of hustle about mobilisation. Some people fled to Germany, some people fled to Croatia, some do their own private business and nobody's forcing them to be mobilised and they will not volunteer to be mobilised. It seems that the HVO military authorities are still very weak." Is this true, and how could any authority, any government be strong given the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the period where for all intents and purposes the Crisis Staff lost any touch with reality and could not manage anything any more and on the other hand the municipal HVO staff operated in the circumstances that prevailed in the town and it is quite logical that issue -- that the issue of mobilisation was not dealt with in accordance with any regulations at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let us look at the 1st of May, 1992. That's page 72. "Two defenders were killed in last night's attacks on Capljina. The Chetniks blew up the bridge on the Neretva in Capljina. At 1700 hours all hell broke loose again in Mostar. The cathedral and the Franciscan monastery were hit. Two persons were killed." Let us look at the 2nd of May 1992. This is a topic that has been discussed at length in this trial. Friar Zovko here talks about his view of international interference and he's talking about fierce fighting in Sarajevo. "European Monitors are warning the Yugoslav army that they will report everything to the European Community in Portugal but the Yugoslav army is not afraid of anyone. The Chetniks are trying to take control of the TV transmitter at Vlasic. Three defenders have been killed and a number of them have been wounded. The Sarajevo TV now covers only Sarajevo because all transmitters in Bosnia are turned towards Belgrade. All PTT links with the world are severed in Bosnia and Herzegovina." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The repeater at Mount Velez that made it possible for Mostar to receive the signal from BH TV was switched off and now faced the other way by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let's look at what Friar Zovko has to say further down. This evening having just returned from Lisbon Alija Izetbegovic was taken prisoner by the Yugoslav People's Army in Sarajevo. And he goes on to say: "A foreign army in a foreign country has taken the country's president prisoner. This is unprecedented. The USA, Germany and Austria responded with mild notes, but Serbs are not afraid of notes. The reaction to the death of the Belgian observer near Cule, that's near Mostar, is far below expectations. Europe and the USA are either totally powerless or do not want to do anything." To your knowledge was this the prevailing feeling among the people regarding all those negotiations, promises that were made, interference, that in fact nobody didn't want to do anything, couldn't do anything against everything that the JNA did? Well, you know yourself, from Vukovar, Dubrovnik, and so on, could you please tell me that.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the question of impotence, unease, pressure, but first of all powerlessness, this is something that was present and it appeared that no help was forthcoming and all the talks at that time, all the agreements that were reached starting with those that were reached while Yugoslavia was still in existence did not yield any results and the people did not expect any help to come from any quarters because it didn't -- nothing, no effort resulted in any protection for the people to give them their homes, jobs, food.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let us look at page 73. The 3rd of May, 1992. "European Monitors are leaving Mostar." It says, "One person was killed and 13 were wounded in the fighting in Mostar last night," and then it goes on to speak about Slavonski Brod which was suffering at the hands of the same aggressors. And then it says that, "Chemical agents were thrown on Siroki Brijeg and the bishop's palace and the hospital in Mostar was fired upon." Did you know that the bishop's palace was almost completely razed to the ground and that hospital was targeted?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And then the 4th of May, 1992 just further down, "Aircraft attack Ljubuski yesterday, killing two and wounding five persons."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you have 10 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, everything here is really the most important, because we would go on -- we should go on day from day to see how the situation developed and then we could talk about reconstructing the events in their entirety.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you please look at the 6th of May, 1992, and that's just one thing I want you to look at. "Bishop's palace set on fire." Do you know that at that time bishop's palace was burnt to the ground and then it says here that, "General Perisic requested that the Mostar HVO and the Territorial Defence withdraw to the right bank of the Neretva River or else he would send aircraft to attack Mostar." Do you know that he was actually blackmailing people into negotiations in this manner?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: The 9th of May, 1992. That's at page 77. "St. Peter and Paul church set on fire." Do you know that this church was burnt to the ground?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: "Ten buses full of women and children left Mostar today as refugees." Is that true that refugees, women and children, were leaving Mostar every day, especially women were desperate to keep their children safe?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to me that was one of the reasons why Mostar was targeted with shells and gunfire to make people leave. And this escalated in particular after the bishop's palace and the St. Peter and Paul church were set on fire and they burnt to the ground.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you please look at page 80. Well, it says, "The Chetniks are firing at Krusevo and Sretnice again and then it says it is peaceful in Mostar. They're hunting for snipers and they have already killed three of them."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note we cannot follow at this speed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I said already that in Centar -- Centar 2 there were such examples and they were hunting snipers down in the buildings.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Were those usually snipers that we found in apartments that were own by the military?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
